facts.raw_span: A 76-year-old woman
history of appendicitis, torsion of an ovarian cyst pedicle, and uterine myoma
rapidly enlarging right parietal mass behind the ear over one month
no neurological deficits or systemic symptoms
laboratory studies, including complete blood counts, metabolic panel, and viral serology for HIV and Epstein-Barr virus, were all normal or negative
Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a 5-cm hyperdense meningeal mass with parietal bone invasion
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the right parietal region
Cerebral angiography demonstrated a vascular tumor supplied by the middle meningeal artery
a clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made
intraoperatively, the tumor was extradural, caused skull destruction, and had no intradural involvement
Histology showed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm
positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin, and negative staining for Epstein-Barr virus

concepts.why: The patient's clinical presentation and imaging studies, including a 5-cm hyperdense meningeal mass with parietal bone invasion on CT and a heterogeneously enhancing lesion on MRI, are consistent with osteoblastic meningioma.
The histological findings of a malignant spindle cell neoplasm with positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin are consistent with this diagnosis.
The patient's clinical presentation and imaging studies could also be consistent with primary lymphoma, although the histological findings do not support this diagnosis.
The patient's clinical presentation and imaging studies could also be consistent with metastasis, although the histological findings do not support this diagnosis.
The patient's clinical presentation and imaging studies could also be consistent with sarcoma, although the histological findings do not support this diagnosis.
The patient's clinical presentation and imaging studies could also be consistent with meningeal hemangiopericytoma, although the histological findings do not support this diagnosis.
The patient's clinical presentation and imaging studies could also be consistent with solitary fibrous tumor, although the histological findings do not support this diagnosis.
The patient's clinical presentation and imaging studies could also be consistent with hemangioma, although the histological findings do not support this diagnosis.
The tumor was extradural, caused skull destruction, and had no intradural involvement, which is consistent with meningeal hemangiopericytoma.
